screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will explore how the Jack OS implements arithmetic operations and basic system services in software. The Hack C P U lacks instructions for multiplication, division, and precise square root, so the Math module provides software algorithms — shift-and-add multiplication, long division with sign handling, and integer square root via binary search or Newton-style iteration. You will also examine the Sys module, which acts as the OS entry point and provides init, halt, error, and a busy-loop wait. These pieces are small but essential: they let higher-level programs perform math and control program execution on hardware that provides only addition, subtraction, bit tests, and memory access. By the end you should be able to explain why shift-and-add is acceptable on a 16-bit Hack, how division handles signs and division-by-zero, and why a busy-wait is used on a machine without timers. Consider: what hardware features would make these routines simpler or faster, and how would that change the OS design?

screens.title: Math.multiply — shift-and-add
screens.narratorSegment: Shift-and-add multiplication is a software technique that builds a product by adding shifted versions of one operand whenever a corresponding bit of the other operand is set. Define the multiplicand x and the multiplier y. Starting with sum = 0 and shiftedX = x, the algorithm inspects each bit of y. If a given bit is set, shiftedX is added into sum. Then shiftedX is doubled (equivalent to a left shift) and we advance to the next bit. On Hack, where hardware shifts are absent, doubling is done by adding a value to itself. For 16-bit integers this loop runs up to 16 times, so complexity is O(n) with n equal to the bit width. A concrete example: multiply 13 by 6. In binary 6 is 110; the algorithm adds x shifted by 1 and by 2 for the set bits, producing 13*2 + 13*4 = 26 + 52 = 78. A common misconception is to expect a single instruction for full-width multiplication; instead, this routine composes shifts and adds and must handle sign and overflow deliberately. The key takeaway is simplicity: it uses only addition and bit testing, which are cheap on Hack. When you implement this in Jack, include tests for 0, 1, negatives, and values near 16-bit limits so you can observe overflow behavior and confirm correctness.

keyIdea.title: Shift-and-add
keyIdea.text: Multiply by adding shifted copies of x when bits of y are set; runs in O(n) for n bits.

content.html:
Core Concept › Math.multiply — shift-and-add

Definition and steps

  1. Initialize sum = 0, shiftedX = x, i = 0.
  2. Repeat for each bit i up to 15: if bit i of y is set, add shiftedX to sum; then set shiftedX = shiftedX + shiftedX; i++.
  3. Return sum as the product.
Key Takeaway

Uses only addition and bit tests, simple to implement on Hack and predictable in iteration count.

Code walkthrough: the canonical Jack implementation is shown for clarity and testing. The comparisons and bit tests use only operations available on Hack.
function int multiply(int x, int y) {
  var int sum, shiftedX, i;
  let sum = 0;
  let shiftedX = x;
  let i = 0;
  while (i < 16) {
    if (y & (1 << i)) {
      let sum = sum + shiftedX;
    }
    let shiftedX = shiftedX + shiftedX;
    let i = i + 1;
  }
  return sum;
}
Concrete example
13 * 6 -> bits 110 -> add 13*2 and 13*4 -> 78
Common mistake
Forgetting to handle signed values or overflow; add explicit tests for negatives and limits.
Pro tip
Use bit tests rather than divisions; doubling by addition stays within core Hack ops.

screens.title: Implementing multiply safely
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing multiply on Hack you must also consider sign and the possibility of overflow. The shift-and-add snippet shown earlier handles the unsigned bit accumulation. To support signed integers, one common approach is to convert operands to positive values, record the final sign, compute the absolute-product with the shift-and-add routine, then apply the sign to the result. For overflow, Hack uses 16-bit arithmetic semantics in Jack; detect when results exceed representable range if your spec requires it, or document wrap-around behavior if not. A concrete example: multiplying -3 by 4. Convert -3 to 3, compute 3*4 = 12, then apply a negative sign to yield -12. A common misconception is that sign propagation can be ignored because bits are tested directly; in two's complement arithmetic you must be explicit about taking absolute values for bit scanning or implement a two's-complement-aware routine. For testing, include operations with one negative operand, both negative operands, and large magnitudes. Also add unit tests for multiply by zero and multiply by one to ensure base cases work. The learner takeaway is to make sign and overflow part of your design checklist rather than an afterthought.

keyIdea.title: Safety checklist
keyIdea.text: Handle signs explicitly, decide on overflow semantics, and include targeted tests for edge cases.

content.html:
Process › Implementing multiply safely

Sign handling pattern

1) Record sign = (x < 0) XOR (y < 0). 2) Convert x and y to absolute values. 3) Run shift-and-add on positives. 4) If sign, negate the product before returning.

Explicitly converting to absolute values avoids scanning sign-extended bits and simplifies logic on small platforms.

Example
-3 * 4: abs(-3) = 3; compute 3*4 = 12; apply negative sign -> -12.

Testing matrix

Base cases
0*x, 1*x, x*1, -1*x
Sign combos
(+,+), (+,-), (-,+), (-,-)
Bounds
Large magnitude near 16-bit limits to observe wrap or overflow.
Regression
Add tests to catch accidental sign-loss after refactors.
Common mistake

Scanning bits of two's-complement values without converting to absolute can yield incorrect partial products when sign bits are set.

screens.title: Math.divide — long division
screens.narratorSegment: Long division in software constructs the quotient by testing whether shifted versions of the divisor fit into the remaining dividend. Begin with a check for division by zero and call Sys. error with an error code if the divisor is zero. To simplify sign handling, reduce signs to positive operands, record the final sign, and apply it to the quotient at the end. The algorithm typically starts with the highest bit position and shifts the divisor left by that bit index; if the shifted divisor is less than or equal to the current dividend, add the corresponding bit to the quotient and subtract the shifted divisor from the dividend. Repeat by decreasing the bit index. This produces the quotient in O(n) iterations for n bits if you check each bit, but each iteration requires a compare and potential subtraction. A concrete example: dividing 77 by 5. Shift 5 left until just under 77, subtract, set quotient bits accordingly, and continue for lower bits until complete. A common misconception is to use repeated subtraction by the original divisor; that naive approach is O(value) and inefficient. Long division is efficient and precise on fixed-width integers and it maps naturally to Hack primitives. When implementing, include sign tests and a clear division-by-zero path so your OS can report the error and halt predictably.

keyIdea.title: Long division
keyIdea.text: Shift the divisor, subtract when it fits, and accumulate bits in the quotient. Detect division-by-zero early.

content.html:
Core Concept › Math.divide — long division

Algorithm steps

  1. Check divisor = 0 -> call Sys.error(3).
  2. Normalize signs and work with absolute values.
  3. For i from highest bit down to 0: set temp = divisor << i; if temp <= dividend then set quotient bit and subtract temp from dividend.
  4. Apply recorded sign to quotient and return.
Concrete example
77 / 5: shift 5 up to 64 (5<<3), subtract 64 -> remainder 13, set bit 3, then handle lower bits to form quotient 15 with remainder 2.

Code snippet

function int divide(int x, int y) {
  var int q, i, temp;
  if (y = 0) {
    do Sys.error(3);
  }
  if ((x < 0) & (y > 0)) { return -Math.divide(-x, y); }
  if ((x > 0) & (y < 0)) { return -Math.divide(x, -y); }
  if ((x < 0) & (y < 0)) { return Math.divide(-x, -y); }

  let q = 0;
  let i = 15;
  while (~(i < 0)) {
    let temp = (y << i);
    if (temp < (x + 1)) {
      let q = q + (1 << i);
      let x = x - temp;
    }
    let i = i - 1;
  }
  return q;
}
Common mistake
Using repeated subtraction by original divisor is too slow for large dividends.
Pro tip
Handle division-by-zero early and standardize sign handling to reuse the positive-case algorithm.

screens.title: Math.sqrt — integer square root
screens.narratorSegment: Computing the integer square root can be done with binary search or with Newton's method. For the Hack platform, binary search is straightforward and predictable. Define low = 0 and high = n + 1. While high - low > 1, pick mid = (low + high) / 2, compute midSquared = mid * mid, then compare to n. If midSquared equals n, return mid; if midSquared is less than n, set low = mid; otherwise set high = mid. When the loop ends low holds the integer floor of the square root. This method is O(log n) in the magnitude of the numeric range derived from bit width and maps neatly to available operations. Handle negative input by calling Sys. error with the designated code. A concrete example: n = 20 yields mid guesses that converge to low = 4, since 4*4 = 16 and 5*5 = 25 which is greater than 20. A common misconception is that Newton's method is always better; while Newton converges faster in floating point, binary search is simpler to implement safely for integer arithmetic on constrained hardware. The takeaway is to pick the approach that balances implementational simplicity and iteration count for the platform at hand.

keyIdea.title: Integer sqrt
keyIdea.text: Binary search gives a robust integer square root and handles edge cases by design.

content.html:
Definition › Math.sqrt — integer square root

Binary search pattern

Initialize low = 0, high = n + 1. While high - low > 1 compute mid and midSquared. Move low or high accordingly. Return low when loop finishes.

Check for negative input first and call Sys.error so programs can fail predictably on invalid input.

Example
n = 20: mids try 10, 5, 3, 4; algorithm returns 4 because 4*4 ≤ 20 < 5*5.

Code (binary search)

function int sqrt(int n) {
  var int low, high, mid, midSquared;
  if (n < 0) { do Sys.error(4); }
  let low = 0;
  let high = n + 1;
  while ((high - low) > 1) {
    let mid = (low + high) / 2;
    let midSquared = mid * mid;
    if (midSquared = n) { return mid; }
    if (midSquared < n) { let low = mid; }
    else { let high = mid; }
  }
  return low;
}
Misconception
Newton is always better — not necessarily for simple integer routines where binary search is clearer and safe.
Pro tip
Return the floor of the root and document behavior for non-perfect squares so callers know to expect integer results.

screens.title: Software arithmetic trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an algorithm for arithmetic on constrained hardware involves weighing simplicity, memory use, and iteration count. Shift-and-add multiplication is O(n) where n is the bit width; for 16-bit integers this means at most 16 additions and checks, which is small and predictable on Hack. Long division and integer square root via binary search both run in roughly O(n) or O(log N) based on bit width; they require compares and shifts but avoid repeated single-step subtraction of the divisor. The chapter contrasts these simple algorithms with advanced methods like Karatsuba or FFT-based multiplication, which reduce asymptotic complexity at the cost of much greater implementation complexity and memory. On Hack, the added complexity is rarely justified because word sizes are small and simplicity aids correctness and understanding. A common learner trap is to assume the asymptotically fastest algorithm is automatically better: instead, match algorithmic complexity to data sizes and platform constraints. The practical takeaway: prefer simple, correct implementations for small-word devices, and reserve complex algorithms for larger word sizes or when profiling shows a real performance need. Software arithmetic trade-offs means on 16-bit hardware, simplicity often beats asymptotic speed; choose algorithms that are easy to verify and test.. In practical terms, complexity and choices for small hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: On 16-bit hardware, simplicity often beats asymptotic speed; choose algorithms that are easy to verify and test.

content.html:
Comparison › Software arithmetic trade-offs

Complexity quick guide

  • Multiply (shift-and-add): O(n) additions and bit checks.
  • Divide (long division): O(n) bit iterations with compares and subtractions.
  • Sqrt (binary search): O(log range) iterations; predictable and safe.
When to optimize
Only consider advanced multiply algorithms when word sizes are large and profiling shows a need. For Hack's 16-bit domain, simplicity is a stronger value than micro-optimization.

Example comparison

Simple
Shift-and-add: easy to implement, test, and reason about for 16 bits.
Complex
Karatsuba/FFT: asymptotically faster but requires more memory and complex transforms.
Misconception

Faster asymptotic complexity always wins — false for small fixed word sizes where constant factors and code complexity matter more.

screens.title: Sys.init and startup sequence
screens.narratorSegment: Sys. init is the entry point that brings the OS and device services to life. Its role is to call initialization routines for Memory, Math, Output, Screen, Keyboard, and any other modules, then call Main. main to start the user's program. Finally it calls Sys. halt to stop execution. This sequence is essential: memory structures need setup, Math utilities may prepare tables, and device-related inits ensure hardware-facing services are ready. Think of Sys. init as a small startup script—a spaceship launch checklist that ensures each subsystem reports ready before the main mission begins. A concrete example is the canonical init that calls Memory. init, Math. init, Output. init, Screen. init, Keyboard. init, then Main. main and Sys. halt. A common misconception is to omit Sys. halt, assuming programs return; on Hack the halt ensures the C P U enters a predictable infinite loop so the machine does not continue executing stray addresses. When you write Sys. init, make the sequence explicit and document the dependency order so future modules can rely on initialized services. Sys.init and startup sequence means sys.init sets up services in a deterministic order, launches main.main, then halts to leave the machine in a known state.. In practical terms, initializing the os and launching main.main. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Sys.init and startup sequence

Sequence

  1. Memory.init()
  2. Math.init()
  3. Output.init(), Screen.init(), Keyboard.init()
  4. Main.main()
  5. Sys.halt()
Analogy
A startup checklist that ensures each subsystem is ready before the main program runs.

Canonical init code

function void init() {
  do Memory.init();
  do Math.init();
  do Output.init();
  do Screen.init();
  do Keyboard.init();
  do Main.main();
  do Sys.halt();
}
Why Sys.halt?
Guarantees the program stops in a controlled infinite loop; avoids executing invalid addresses after main returns.
Dependency note
Order matters: Memory.init should precede modules that allocate or store state.

screens.title: Sys.halt and Sys.error
screens.narratorSegment: Sys. halt provides a reliable program termination by entering an infinite loop. On simple hardware like Hack, halting ensures the C P U does not proceed to execute arbitrary memory. Sys. error prints an error code and then halts the machine; it is used to signal fatal runtime conditions such as division by zero or a negative square-root input. When designing Sys. error pick compact error codes that callers can document and tests can assert. A concrete example: Math. divide calls Sys. error(3) when dividing by zero; Math. sqrt calls Sys. error(4) for negative inputs. A common misconception is to treat errors as recoverable without explicit design; on Hack, many errors are fatal because there is no process abstraction or exception handling. The learner takeaway is to provide predictable, documented failure modes and to keep error handling simple and deterministic so unit tests can rely on them. Make sure printed messages or codes are consistent and that tests assert the expected error code and halting behavior. Sys.halt and Sys.error means sys.error reports a code and halts; sys.halt ensures a well-defined stop state on minimal hardware.. In practical terms, program termination and clear error reporting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Sys.halt and Sys.error

Sys.error workflow

Sys.error(code) should print or expose the error code and then call Sys.halt to stop execution. Use distinct codes for different fatal conditions so tests can verify the exact cause.

Example codes from the chapter: 3 for division by zero, 4 for negative sqrt input.

Key Takeaway

Fatal errors are handled deterministically: report then halt so behavior is testable on Hack.

Sys.halt

Sys.halt simply enters an infinite loop. It is the canonical termination mechanism on Hack. Tests should expect execution to stop and not return to caller code.

Test idea
Trigger Sys.error and assert the reported code and that execution does not continue.
Misconception
Assuming a halted machine can resume — on Hack halt is final until reset.

screens.title: Sys.wait — busy-loop timing
screens.narratorSegment: Sys. wait implements a delay by running nested loops that iterate a prescribed number of times. The routine increments counters in an inner loop to consume C P U cycles and an outer loop to adjust total duration. This busy loop is simple and portable because Hack lacks hardware timers and interrupt support. For example, Sys. wait(duration) runs an outer loop from i = 0 to duration, and an inner loop that increments j until it reaches a fixed bound, thereby creating an approximate delay. The important caveat is that busy waiting uses 100 percent of the C P U while it runs, so it is unsuitable for multitasking or energy-sensitive contexts. A common misconception is to expect exact timing from busy loops; actual delay depends on C P U clock and instruction timings. For tests, run Sys. wait with different durations and observe relative delays rather than relying on absolute timings. The learner takeaway is to accept busy-waiting as a pragmatic but inefficient solution on minimal hardware and to consider hardware timers and interrupts as the correct alternative on real systems.

keyIdea.text: A portable but inefficient delay: predictable in structure, imprecise in duration and CPU-heavy.

content.html:
Process Flow › Sys.wait — busy-loop timing

Implementation pattern

function void wait(int duration) {
  var int i, j;
  let i = 0;
  while (i < duration) {
    let j = 0;
    while (j < 100) {
      let j = j + 1;
    }
    let i = i + 1;
  }
  return;
}

Inner loop bound (100 above) sets granularity. Increase or decrease to adjust per-iteration cost when calibrating on actual hardware.

Pros and cons

Pros
Portable, simple to implement, no hardware dependencies.
Cons
Consumes full CPU, imprecise timing, unsuitable for multitasking.
Test idea
Run wait with durations 1, 2, 5 and measure relative pauses to confirm scaling.

screens.title: Memory allocator choices
screens.narratorSegment: Memory management on the Hack platform is simplified because programs have modest memory needs, but allocator design still matters. A simple linked-list allocator tracks free blocks and services allocation requests by walking the list for a fit; it is easy to implement and requires little metadata. To reduce fragmentation one can implement coalescing (merging adjacent free blocks) or use segregated free lists that keep separate lists for common block sizes. These approaches reduce fragmentation and allocation time at the cost of more bookkeeping. For Hack, the chapter recommends a simple linked-list allocator as sufficient because workload and memory are small. A common misconception is to believe more complex allocators are always better; in small systems the overhead of complex metadata and management can outweigh runtime benefits. The practical takeaway: choose the simplest allocator that meets performance and fragmentation needs, and document assumptions about typical allocation patterns so future maintainers understand the trade-offs. Memory allocator choices means simple linked lists minimize complexity; segregated lists and coalescing reduce fragmentation but require more metadata and logic.. In practical terms, linked list allocator vs. segregated free lists and coalescing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Core Concept › Memory allocator choices

Simple linked-list allocator

Maintain a linked list of free blocks. On allocation, walk the list to find a suitable block and split if necessary. On free, add the block back to the list and optionally coalesce with neighbors.

Advantages: small code size, easy to reason about. Disadvantages: potential fragmentation and linear allocation time.

Segregated lists and coalescing

Segregated lists hold free blocks by size class to speed allocation. Coalescing merges adjacent free blocks to reduce fragmentation. Both reduce long-term fragmentation at the cost of metadata and complexity.

For Hack the chapter recommends starting simple and optimizing only if real workloads show fragmentation or performance issues.

Test idea
Allocate and free various sizes in patterns that mimic your programs and measure free memory over time to detect fragmentation.

Assessment › Explain complexity & justify choices

Sample question

"The shift-and-add multiplication algorithm has time complexity O(n) where n is number of bits. For 16-bit integers this requires up to 16 iterations. Why is this acceptable for the Hack computer, and what would be a faster algorithm for larger integers?"

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will explore how the Jack OS implements arithmetic operations and basic system services in software. The Hack C P U lacks instructions for multiplication, division, and precise square root, so the Math module provides software algorithms — shift-and-add multiplication, long division with sign handling, and integer square root via binary search or Newton-style iteration. You will also examine the Sys module, which acts as the OS entry point and provides init, halt, error, and a busy-loop wait. These pieces are small but essential: they let higher-level programs perform math and control program execution on hardware that provides only addition, subtraction, bit tests, and memory access. We will ground each algorithm with code examples, edge-case tests, and practical trade-offs for performance and simplicity. By the end you should be able to explain why shift-and-add is acceptable on a 16-bit Hack, how division handles signs and division-by-zero, and why a busy-wait is used on a machine without timers. Consider: what hardware features would make these routines simpler or faster, and how would that change the OS design?

By the end of these screens you will be able to implement and reason about the Math and Sys modules in the Jack OS. First, you will implement multiplication as a shift-and-add routine, learn to test it with zero, one, negative values, and boundary cases, and understand why 16 iterations suffices for 16-bit integers. Second, you will implement division as a long-division algorithm that handles signs and raises an error on division by zero; you will see how to build the quotient bit by bit. Third, you will compute integer square roots using binary search, with checks for negative inputs. Finally, you will implement the Sys module functions that initialize services, halt execution, report errors, and busy-wait. Each objective pairs a concrete implementation task with tests and a short explanation of performance trade-offs so you can justify design decisions in code reviews or exams.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on tasks and the reasoning behind them. You will test multiply with zeros, ones, negative operands and values near the 16-bit limit to spot overflow behavior. For divide, you will include division-by-zero tests that exercise Sys. error and a set of sign-pair tests so you can observe how the algorithm reduces negatives to positive cases. For sqrt, you will test perfect squares, non-perfect squares, zero, one, and negative inputs that must trigger an error. You will implement Sys. wait and verify approximate timing for different durations; understand that the busy loop wastes C P U cycles and is only suitable for simple delays on Hack. Finally, you will compare recursive versus loop Fibonacci implementations to see the performance cost of repeated function calls versus iterative accumulation. These testing tasks teach not only correctness but also how to reason about complexity and choose appropriate algorithms for small hardware.

Shift-and-add multiplication is a software technique that builds a product by adding shifted versions of one operand whenever a corresponding bit of the other operand is set. Define the multiplicand x and the multiplier y. Starting with sum = 0 and shiftedX = x, the algorithm inspects each bit of y. If a given bit is set, shiftedX is added into sum. Then shiftedX is doubled (equivalent to a left shift) and we advance to the next bit. On Hack, where hardware shifts are absent, doubling is done by adding a value to itself. For 16-bit integers this loop runs up to 16 times, so complexity is O(n) with n equal to the bit width. A concrete example: multiply 13 by 6. In binary 6 is 110; the algorithm adds x shifted by 1 and by 2 for the set bits, producing 13*2 + 13*4 = 26 + 52 = 78. A common misconception is to expect a single instruction for full-width multiplication; instead, this routine composes shifts and adds and must handle sign and overflow deliberately. The key takeaway is simplicity: it uses only addition and bit testing, which are cheap on Hack. When you implement this in Jack, include tests for 0, 1, negatives, and values near 16-bit limits so you can observe overflow behavior and confirm correctness.

When implementing multiply on Hack you must also consider sign and the possibility of overflow. The shift-and-add snippet shown earlier handles the unsigned bit accumulation. To support signed integers, one common approach is to convert operands to positive values, record the final sign, compute the absolute-product with the shift-and-add routine, then apply the sign to the result. For overflow, Hack uses 16-bit arithmetic semantics in Jack; detect when results exceed representable range if your spec requires it, or document wrap-around behavior if not. A concrete example: multiplying -3 by 4. Convert -3 to 3, compute 3*4 = 12, then apply a negative sign to yield -12. A common misconception is that sign propagation can be ignored because bits are tested directly; in two's complement arithmetic you must be explicit about taking absolute values for bit scanning or implement a two's-complement-aware routine. For testing, include operations with one negative operand, both negative operands, and large magnitudes. Also add unit tests for multiply by zero and multiply by one to ensure base cases work. The learner takeaway is to make sign and overflow part of your design checklist rather than an afterthought.

Long division in software constructs the quotient by testing whether shifted versions of the divisor fit into the remaining dividend. Begin with a check for division by zero and call Sys. error with an error code if the divisor is zero. To simplify sign handling, reduce signs to positive operands, record the final sign, and apply it to the quotient at the end. The algorithm typically starts with the highest bit position and shifts the divisor left by that bit index; if the shifted divisor is less than or equal to the current dividend, add the corresponding bit to the quotient and subtract the shifted divisor from the dividend. Repeat by decreasing the bit index. This produces the quotient in O(n) iterations for n bits if you check each bit, but each iteration requires a compare and potential subtraction. A concrete example: dividing 77 by 5. Shift 5 left until just under 77, subtract, set quotient bits accordingly, and continue for lower bits until complete. A common misconception is to use repeated subtraction by the original divisor; that naive approach is O(value) and inefficient. Long division is efficient and precise on fixed-width integers and it maps naturally to Hack primitives. When implementing, include sign tests and a clear division-by-zero path so your OS can report the error and halt predictably.

Computing the integer square root can be done with binary search or with Newton's method. For the Hack platform, binary search is straightforward and predictable. Define low = 0 and high = n + 1. While high - low > 1, pick mid = (low + high) / 2, compute midSquared = mid * mid, then compare to n. If midSquared equals n, return mid; if midSquared is less than n, set low = mid; otherwise set high = mid. When the loop ends low holds the integer floor of the square root. This method is O(log n) in the magnitude of the numeric range derived from bit width and maps neatly to available operations. Handle negative input by calling Sys. error with the designated code. A concrete example: n = 20 yields mid guesses that converge to low = 4, since 4*4 = 16 and 5*5 = 25 which is greater than 20. A common misconception is that Newton's method is always better; while Newton converges faster in floating point, binary search is simpler to implement safely for integer arithmetic on constrained hardware. The takeaway is to pick the approach that balances implementational simplicity and iteration count for the platform at hand.

Choosing an algorithm for arithmetic on constrained hardware involves weighing simplicity, memory use, and iteration count. Shift-and-add multiplication is O(n) where n is the bit width; for 16-bit integers this means at most 16 additions and checks, which is small and predictable on Hack. Long division and integer square root via binary search both run in roughly O(n) or O(log N) based on bit width; they require compares and shifts but avoid repeated single-step subtraction of the divisor. The chapter contrasts these simple algorithms with advanced methods like Karatsuba or FFT-based multiplication, which reduce asymptotic complexity at the cost of much greater implementation complexity and memory. On Hack, the added complexity is rarely justified because word sizes are small and simplicity aids correctness and understanding. A common learner trap is to assume the asymptotically fastest algorithm is automatically better: instead, match algorithmic complexity to data sizes and platform constraints. The practical takeaway: prefer simple, correct implementations for small-word devices, and reserve complex algorithms for larger word sizes or when profiling shows a real performance need. Software arithmetic trade-offs means on 16-bit hardware, simplicity often beats asymptotic speed; choose algorithms that are easy to verify and test.. In practical terms, complexity and choices for small hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Sys. init is the entry point that brings the OS and device services to life. Its role is to call initialization routines for Memory, Math, Output, Screen, Keyboard, and any other modules, then call Main. main to start the user's program. Finally it calls Sys. halt to stop execution. This sequence is essential: memory structures need setup, Math utilities may prepare tables, and device-related inits ensure hardware-facing services are ready. Think of Sys. init as a small startup script—a spaceship launch checklist that ensures each subsystem reports ready before the main mission begins. A concrete example is the canonical init that calls Memory. init, Math. init, Output. init, Screen. init, Keyboard. init, then Main. main and Sys. halt. A common misconception is to omit Sys. halt, assuming programs return; on Hack the halt ensures the C P U enters a predictable infinite loop so the machine does not continue executing stray addresses. When you write Sys. init, make the sequence explicit and document the dependency order so future modules can rely on initialized services. Sys. halt provides a reliable program termination by entering an infinite loop. On simple hardware like Hack, halting ensures the C P U does not proceed to execute arbitrary memory. Sys. wait implements a delay by running nested loops that iterate a prescribed number of times. The routine increments counters in an inner loop to consume C P U cycles and an outer loop to adjust total duration. This busy loop is simple and portable because Hack lacks hardware timers and interrupt support. For example, Sys. wait(duration) runs an outer loop from i = 0 to duration, and an inner loop that increments j until it reaches a fixed bound, thereby creating an approximate delay. The important caveat is that busy waiting uses 100 percent of the C P U while it runs, so it is unsuitable for multitasking or energy-sensitive contexts. A common misconception is to expect exact timing from busy loops; actual delay depends on C P U clock and instruction timings. For tests, run Sys. wait with different durations and observe relative delays rather than relying on absolute timings. The learner takeaway is to accept busy-waiting as a pragmatic but inefficient solution on minimal hardware and to consider hardware timers and interrupts as the correct alternative on real systems.

Memory management on the Hack platform is simplified because programs have modest memory needs, but allocator design still matters. A simple linked-list allocator tracks free blocks and services allocation requests by walking the list for a fit; it is easy to implement and requires little metadata. To reduce fragmentation one can implement coalescing (merging adjacent free blocks) or use segregated free lists that keep separate lists for common block sizes. These approaches reduce fragmentation and allocation time at the cost of more bookkeeping.
